reviews.pullQuote: Ouro UI declares an action once, and that one action becomes a person's button and an agent's tool on web, Apple, Windows and Android, with consent built in.
reviews.testimonial: I'd pick Ouro UI because it was designed for this exact brief: things that people and agents both use, on more than one platform. Its one action model generates a CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, a web control, an App Intent and a SwiftUI button from a single declaration, and CI fails if any of them drift. Its consent classes (read, write, consequential, person-only) carry into the composed-UI tree that each native kit draws, so an agent can't relabel a button or loosen what a press is allowed to do. The real trade-off is maturity compared with A2UI. A2UI has a v1.0 protocol, official renderers for Flutter, React, Lit, Angular and SwiftUI, and a Compose renderer published through AndroidX. Ouro is a tiny project, and its Android and Windows kits have eight components each at v0.3. Ouro also reads A2UI messages on web and Apple, which keeps a way out open if I need one.
reviews.evaluations:
**Ouro UI** — My pick. It's the only candidate built as a complete system where one declaration serves both a person and an agent. In the [core actions guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), `defineAction` takes a consent class (read, write, consequential or person-only) and generates the CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, a web control, an App Intent, a SwiftUI `Button(intent:)` and a Reins action. CI fails when a generated file drifts from its declaration. The [composed-UI guide](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/) defines a validated data tree. Each button in it must be one of your declared actions, and the validator refuses a tree that relabels a button or loosens its consent. Web, SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and Compose all draw the tree natively, and it also reaches people through MCP Apps hosts and A2UI messages. The web kit has 125 components on Base UI, delivered as a shadcn registry, and the [Apple package](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) is at 1.x with source-stable APIs. The project documents its own gaps, and I saw them. The [Android page](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) says Android has eight composables at v0.3.0, has been checked only on emulators, refuses consequential actions for now, and isn't on Maven Central. The Windows kit is also at v0.3. Android and Windows read the tree but not A2UI. Adoption is the biggest risk: the [org page](https://github.com/ourostack) shows a single small team with almost no stars, so bus factor is real. What would ease that: Android/Windows kits closer to web's component count, real-device testing, Maven Central publishing, and outside adopters beyond Spoonjoy. One caution: the project publishes its own "model reviews". I based this choice on the architecture, not on those pages.

**A2UI** — The strongest alternative, and my hedge. The [README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui) describes declarative UI-as-data with catalog validation, streaming, and agent SDKs in Python, TypeScript and Dart. The [SDK page](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) lists official renderers for Flutter, React, Lit, Angular and SwiftUI, plus Jetpack Compose via AndroidX (v0.9.1). It maps protocol accessibility to each platform's native APIs. That's the broadest native reach of any agent-UI protocol here. The trade-off: it covers agents composing UI for people, not agents *using* your app through the same actions. It's a protocol and catalog, not a design system, so I'd still need components and an action/consent layer on top. If I needed vendor-backed maturity above all, I'd choose it, and Ouro's A2UI adapter keeps that door open.

**MCP Apps** — A standard extension for MCP tools to return `ui://` HTML resources. Hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, with two-way postMessage calls to tools. It's supported in Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose and others ([README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)). It's excellent for distributing UI into chat hosts, but it's a delivery channel built on web iframes, with no native rendering and no design system. I'd use it as one output format, which Ouro already does, rather than as the toolkit.

**CopilotKit** — A strong agent-to-frontend runtime: AG-UI streaming, shared state, human-in-the-loop, frontend tools, WebMCP, and generative UI via registered components, A2UI or MCP Apps. Surfaces include React (GA), Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). It's centred on connecting an agent backend to a copilot, and it isn't a visual design system. It has no SwiftUI or Compose path, and parts of the production story (Intelligence, Soar) are commercial. Pair it with a design system if your app is chat- or copilot-centric.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its architecture closely matches Ouro's action idea. One `defineAction` serves the UI hooks, the agent tool, HTTP, MCP, A2A and the CLI, all with shared validation, access checks and audit ([actions overview](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview)). But it's a full-stack TypeScript/React app framework (Nitro, Postgres), not a design system. I saw no native iOS or Android kit and no consent-class model like Ouro's person-only refusal. Choose it for web-first agent apps where you want the whole backend.

**json-render** — A catalog-guardrailed generative UI framework with Zod component and action schemas and streaming specs. Renderers cover React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, PDF, email, Ink, Slack/Teams cards and MCP Apps ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). It reaches the most output targets of anything here. Its native path, though, is React Native rather than SwiftUI or Compose. It's also agent-to-person generation, without an agent-uses-the-app action model or consent semantics.

**AI Elements** — The [README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) says it's deprecated at the end of November 2026 and moving into shadcn/ui. It's web-only chat and agent-trace components. I wouldn't start a project on it.

**shadcn/ui** — Copy-in open code with a registry, an MCP server and llms.txt, which makes it very legible to coding agents. It now hosts the AI Elements patterns (Tool, Confirmation, Plan, Trace) ([AI Elements docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements)). It's web/React only, and it covers chat-UI patterns rather than a shared action model. It's a great base layer, which is why Ouro's web half ships through its registry.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tailwind 4 tokens and Radix-based accessible React components tuned for ChatGPT apps ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). It's narrowly scoped to one host's look, with no native targets and no agent action model.

**Vercel UI SDK** — Headless behaviors (focus, selection, popups, drag and drop, ARIA) with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. It's designed for agents to assemble components, and the [docs](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs) mention WebMCP and letting agents call component actions. It's an interesting web primitive layer, but it's in beta and has no native platforms.

**Radix UI** — Mature, accessible, unstyled React primitives ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). They're a web foundation only, with nothing for agents or native.

**Base UI** — The modern unstyled successor from the Radix, Floating UI and MUI people ([README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)). Ouro's web components are built on it. It's still web-only, and its README describes nothing agent-specific.

**MUI** — A battle-tested Material Design React library ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). It's comprehensive for web dashboards, but has no native kit and no agent semantics.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Arguably the best-in-class accessibility and internationalization for the web. React Stately is described as usable on other platforms ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). There's no native rendering and no agent layer. I'd value it as a reference for a11y rigor.

**Chakra UI** — An accessible React component system that ships an MCP server for coding agents ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). It's web-only, and that MCP server helps agents *build with* Chakra, not agents *use* your app.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's design system as React v9, v8 and Web Components ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). This repo is web only. Native Fluent lives elsewhere, and there's no agent action model here.

**Tamagui** — Shares React and React Native UI through an optimizing compiler ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). It offers real cross-platform reach within React, but it renders through React Native rather than SwiftUI or Compose, and it has no agent features.

**Flutter** — One codebase for mobile, web and desktop with full pixel control ([README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). A2UI has an official Flutter renderer. Still, Flutter draws its own widgets rather than the platform's, and it gives no shared action or consent model for agents. You'd have to assemble that yourself.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — The best toolkit for native Android, with deep Material 3 theming and semantics-based accessibility ([docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). It's single-platform. Agent access comes from separate Android features like AppFunctions, which Ouro's Android kit generates for.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The native Apple toolkit across iOS, macOS, visionOS and watchOS, with strong accessibility ([docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). Agent access comes through App Intents, which Ouro generates from its declarations. On its own it's Apple-only and gives you no web half.
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

reviews.pullQuote: Ouro UI declares an action once, so a person presses it and an agent calls it, with consent built in. It ships native kits for web, Apple, Windows and Android.
reviews.testimonial: I'd choose Ouro UI because it treats people and agents as co-users of one surface. Its one-action declaration generates a CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, an App Intent and a SwiftUI button. Its consent classes also stop an agent from running a consequential action unconfirmed. It has native kits for React, SwiftUI, WinUI and Compose, and it accepts MCP Apps and A2UI payloads. The trade-off is maturity. It is a small project, and its benchmarks and model reviews are self-published. A2UI or MCP Apps carry far more ecosystem weight, so I'd verify Ouro's claims in a pilot first.
reviews.evaluations:
**Base UI** — An unstyled, accessible component library from the creators of Radix, Floating UI and Material UI ([README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)). It is a solid, headless web layer. The README describes no agent-invocation model and no native story. It would need a separate action layer and native kits to meet this brief.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's design system, with React v9 (used by Microsoft 365), legacy v8, and Web Components ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). It is mature and accessible. This repo is web-only, and the README describes no agent-facing contract. The Web Components package is still versioned as beta in the README.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tailwind 4 tokens plus Radix-based React components for ChatGPT apps ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). It is good for the look and feel of UI inside ChatGPT. It is React-only and has no native kit. Its README documents no action or agent-tool model, so pair it with MCP Apps.

**MCP Apps** — An MCP extension where tools declare `ui://` HTML resources. The host renders them in a sandboxed iframe, and the UI can call tools back through the host ([README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)). It has broad host support (ChatGPT, Claude, VS Code, Goose). It is a delivery protocol, not a design system, and it is webview-based, so it is not native. It is the right transport layer, not the whole toolkit.

**AI Elements** — A shadcn-based set of chat components for AI SDK apps. Its own README warns that it will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 in favor of shadcn/ui's version ([README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)). Do not start new work on it.

**MUI** — A comprehensive React implementation of Material Design, extended by MUI X ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). It is battle-tested for web UI. It is web-only and has no agent-facing contract in its README. It suits human dashboards, not cross-platform agent surfaces.

**Chakra UI** — An accessible React component system. It ships an MCP server package (`@chakra-ui/react-mcp`) so coding agents can read its docs ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). That helps agents that author UI. It does not help agents operate the UI, and it is web-only.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — An action-centric framework. `defineAction` with a zod schema becomes an agent tool, a UI call, and HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI surfaces, with shared state and approvals ([README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)). Its architecture is the closest to Ouro's one-action idea. It is not a component or design system, and it is TypeScript and web centered with no native kits.

**Flutter** — A single-codebase UI SDK for mobile, web and desktop, with Material and Cupertino widgets ([README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). It is strong for native reach, and A2UI has a Flutter renderer. It has no built-in agent-action or consent model, so you would add one. Its custom rendering is also less transparent than DOM semantics to browser-based agents.

**Tamagui** — Shares code across React and React Native through an optimizing compiler ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). It is good for web plus iOS and Android. Its README documents no agent features and no SwiftUI, Compose or Windows targets.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Google's Android-native design system and toolkit, with theming, accessibility semantics and a large component set ([docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). It is excellent for Android. It is Android-only and has no agent contract by itself. Ouro's Android kit shows Compose can host one.

**CopilotKit** — A full-stack agent UI stack over AG-UI, with chat, generative UI, shared state and human-in-the-loop. It supports A2UI and MCP Apps, and targets React, Angular, Vue and React Native, plus Slack and Teams ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). It is very capable for putting agents in front of users. It is not a design system, it has no SwiftUI or Compose kits, and it has commercial add-ons.

**Radix UI** — Low-level accessible React primitives for design systems ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). It is a good base layer, and other candidates (Apps SDK UI, shadcn) build on it. It is web-only and has no agent layer.

**Vercel UI SDK** — A beta library of framework-agnostic behaviors (focus, selection, popups, ARIA). It has React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Component adapters and an agent skill, so agents author UI with it ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)). It is an interesting design for agent authors. It is web-only and in beta under Vercel's beta terms, and it does not cover agent invocation of the UI.

**shadcn/ui** — Copy-in components you own, described as something to "build your own component library" ([README](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui)). Its registry format underlies AI Elements and Ouro HX. It is a flexible web foundation. It is web-only, and its README says nothing about agent actions or native platforms.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Apple's declarative framework across iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS and visionOS, with accessibility APIs ([docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). It is the authoritative native Apple path. It covers Apple only. A2UI and Ouro both target it as a renderer for cross-platform agent UI.

**json-render** — A Vercel Labs generative UI framework. You define a zod catalog, the AI emits a JSON spec, and renderers exist for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, PDF, email and others. It also has an MCP integration ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). It is guardrailed and broad. Its native coverage is React Native only, and its README documents no consent or action-parity model.

**Ouro UI** — My pick. It has two halves: Ouro HX, shadcn-format React components, and Ouro AX, a CLI, API and MCP kit with an X-ray conformance checker. Agent-composed UI is validated as data against your catalog. Actions are declared once and generated into CLI, MCP, WebMCP, App Intent and button forms, with consent classes and typed refusals. It has native kits for SwiftUI, WinUI and Compose, and it accepts MCP Apps and A2UI payloads ([README](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui)). Risks: it is young, the Android kit is checked on emulators only, there is no Flutter or React Native path by design, and the benchmark and model-review evidence is self-published. An independent pilot would settle that.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Unstyled accessible components, React Stately state hooks, and Adobe's Spectrum implementation. It has strong internationalization and adaptive interaction ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). It is the best web accessibility base here, and accessibility semantics also help agents. It has no agent-action layer, and it is web-first (Stately can be reused on other platforms).

**A2UI** — A protocol that expresses UI as validated data, streamed from agents to native renderers. Renderers exist for Lit, Angular, React and Flutter, and there are agent SDKs for Python and TypeScript ([README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui)). It is the strongest open standard for cross-platform generative UI, with a clear trust boundary. It is not a human-facing design system, and it does not unify the actions a person presses with the tools an agent calls. That is Ouro's differentiator, and Ouro can consume A2UI.
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

reviews.pullQuote: I’d choose Ouro UI because people and agents can use the same declared actions without giving the agent control of the person’s screen.
reviews.testimonial: I’d choose Ouro UI for a product that needs both native screens and agent-callable actions. Its one action model generates human controls and agent tool definitions from the same declaration, and Composed UI takes an ActionButton’s label and consent rules from the app’s trusted catalog, not the model. I’d use the Ouro AX X-ray to check the exposed interfaces in CI, alongside end-to-end approval tests. A2UI offers a more portable composition protocol, and Ouro’s Windows and Android kits are much narrower than its web kit, so I’d start with web and Apple and validate the other targets on real devices before committing.
reviews.evaluations:
**shadcn/ui** — The CLI copies editable source into the app, and the registry can distribute a team’s components, hooks, and rules. Its MCP server helps coding agents discover and install those assets; its AI Elements patterns help people review tool calls and plans. Neither makes a product operation callable by an agent at runtime. I’d use it for the web component layer and pair it with explicit action contracts and native implementations. [Registry MCP documentation](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp) · [AI Elements patterns](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — `defineAction()` is a shared server implementation for React hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, with common validation and access checks. That’s compelling for a web workspace where the two actors also share application data. Its runtime-generated inline UI runs Alpine/Tailwind code in a sandboxed iframe, rather than composing a catalog of native controls. I’d use the shared action layer if building that kind of workspace, but would need separate native clients and a constrained renderer for this project. [Actions overview](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) · [Generative UI](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/generative-ui.md).

**json-render** — `defineCatalog` gives the model a vocabulary, `defineRegistry` maps it to concrete widgets and handlers, and SpecStream supports progressive rendering. It’s attractive for an existing TypeScript product that needs React Native and multiple web renderers without adopting an agent backend. The catalog constrains what the model can request; the handlers still own authorization and consequential-action approval. I’d consider it with a shared approval layer and renderer parity tests. [Registry and handlers](https://json-render.dev/docs/registry#action-handlers) · [SpecStream documentation](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render#streaming-specstream).

**MCP Apps** — SEP-1865 links tools to predeclared `ui://` HTML resources and gives sandboxed views a bidirectional JSON-RPC bridge to the host. I’d choose it to distribute an interactive tool across compliant chat hosts. It standardizes embedding rather than native widget composition or app-wide consent, and host support is negotiated. I’d ship structured or text fallbacks and test each intended host. [SEP-1865](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx).

**MUI** — Material UI provides a ready-made React component library with theme-level defaults, slot overrides, and variants; MUI X adds more complex widgets. That’s a strong fit for a data-heavy web console. The non-tree-shakable theme is a concrete reason to prefer dedicated wrappers for heavy customizations. For this project I’d use those wrappers as render targets behind an action catalog, not expect the components or theme to supply agent permissions or native parity. [Themed components](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theme-components/) · [Material UI repository](https://github.com/mui/material-ui).

**Chakra UI** — `createSystem`, semantic tokens, and slot recipes let a React team standardize styling centrally; `strictTokens` can enforce token usage with generated TypeScript types. The MCP server gives coding agents component APIs and examples, not access to the resulting product’s actions. I’d use Chakra to build the web UI quickly if I already had a runtime action layer and a separate native rendering plan. [Theming architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview) · [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server.mdx).

**AI Elements** — The standalone Vercel registry copies AI SDK-oriented React components such as Conversation and Message into the app, so existing teams keep their customizations. It saves work on the transcript, not on execution, authorization, or native rendering. The repository announces end-of-November 2026 deprecation, and shadcn already documents the replacement patterns and their migration gaps. For a new project I’d start there rather than adopt the standalone registry. [Standalone README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) · [Replacement and migration guide](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements).

**Ouro UI** — The one action model generates control and tool bindings from declared operations; Composed UI validates the tree against the catalog and rejects changes to an action button’s label or consent class. `ax-xray` checks the exposed interfaces from the outside, which is useful alongside workflow tests, not a replacement for them. The composed catalog is smaller than the web kit, and Windows and Android read Ouro’s tree rather than A2UI messages. Android documents emulator-only validation and Windows documents a client-runtime test gap. I’d verify approval and refusal end to end on actual devices, enforce authorization at the action handler, and expand native coverage only as needed. [Composed UI](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/) · [One action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) · [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) · [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) · [X-ray](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/ax-conformance/).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A packaged React design system with Tailwind 4 tokens, Radix-based components, and dark-mode utilities gives ChatGPT embeds a consistent look. The UI package isn’t the MCP host bridge or a native renderer. I’d use it for a ChatGPT-first app and keep domain actions in host-independent MCP tools so the presentation can change without rewriting those actions. [Apps SDK UI README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui).

**Tamagui** — `@tamagui/core` shares typed tokens and styling across React and React Native; the optional `@tamagui/static` compiler extracts atomic CSS and flattens eligible components, with a runtime fallback. I’d favor it if reusing the same web and mobile component source were paramount. The compiler adds build integration, and the shared component code doesn’t itself define what an agent can discover or execute. I’d pair it with a runtime catalog and shared action policy. [Tamagui architecture](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — React Stately separates state from React Aria’s interaction behavior; Spectrum supplies themed components on top. That split makes keyboard behavior, screen-reader support, and internationalization reusable without forcing Adobe’s visual design. Unstyled Aria still needs visual design work, and shared state hooks don’t provide native widgets or a runtime agent contract. I’d use Aria for accessibility-sensitive web widgets behind a constrained catalog and test the rendered flows with assistive technology. [Architecture RFC](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum/blob/main/rfcs/2019-v3-architecture.md) · [Package overview](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum).

**Fluent UI** — React v9 uses slots and trigger composition, while the repository separately maintains React v8 and Web Components. This is a practical UI layer for Microsoft-aligned products, and v8/v9 coexistence enables gradual migration, but coexistence is not a single component API. I’d standardize new app code on v9 and add an independent domain-action layer; the slots don’t define what an agent may do. [Project and version overview](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) · [v9 slots and triggers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/shows/fluent-ui-insights/fluent-ui-insights-apis-in-v9-slots-jsx-children-triggers).

**Vercel UI SDK** — `definePrimitive` and `createParts` separate reusable focus, selection, and popup behaviors from five web adapters. Unlike a build-time-only assistant integration, `createAgent` gives runtime agents `snapshot`, `query`, and `act` over component APIs, with permission hooks and optional WebMCP exposure. That’s useful for manipulating a visible browser interface; I’d still expose domain operations separately so they don’t depend on what’s mounted. I’d also regression-test any beta API I pinned. [UI SDK quickstart](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs) · [Runtime agent bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Declarative views, scenes, modifiers, and UIKit/AppKit interop are a direct route to Apple-native experiences; the HIG guides platform-specific behavior, and App Intents separately exposes structured actions to Siri and Shortcuts. I’d choose this for an Apple-only app. For this comparison, I’d need to map those intents to the same action contracts used on web and Android; Apple’s framework does not provide those targets. [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) · [Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines) · [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents).

**Base UI** — Unstyled React parts support an element or function `render` prop, with documented merging of event handlers, refs, and attributes. That gives a design-system team precise control over markup, but custom renderers have to preserve the primitive’s accessibility behavior and supply styling. I’d use it as a web substrate behind a curated catalog, not as the catalog, native renderer, or action policy itself. [Composition handbook](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition).

**A2UI** — The transport-independent v1.0 protocol separates component and data-model updates, supports catalog-validated function calls, and leaves styling to the host renderer. I’d choose it if independently implemented agents and clients needed to exchange native UI descriptions. The SDK matrix documents v1.0 for Flutter, web, and SwiftUI, but v0.9.1 for Jetpack Compose, so I’d negotiate versions and test the common catalog. I prefer Ouro here because I want consent and person-only handoff expressed in the same declarations as product actions; with A2UI I’d implement that policy above the protocol. [v1.0 specification](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) · [SDK version matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/).

**Radix UI** — Radix Primitives supplies low-level React interactions; `asChild` composes those behaviors onto an existing DOM element. Custom leaves must spread props and forward refs, and swapping the element can cost accessibility if it stops being focusable. I’d use tested Radix wrappers for web dialogs and menus, then add a separate action contract and native mappings. [Radix composition guide](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition).

**CopilotKit** — Copilot Runtime and AG-UI connect existing agents to frontend tools, streamed state, chat, and generative UI. `useHumanInTheLoop` lets the model ask for input through a registered tool; `useInterrupt` lets agent code enforce a pause. I’d choose it for embedding a copilot in an existing product. The docs note that interrupts are unavailable on the Built-in Agent at this snapshot; for a mandatory checkpoint I’d use a backend with interrupt support and enforce approval in the operation itself. [Architecture](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit#how-it-works) · [Human-in-the-loop patterns](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native/google-antigravity/human-in-the-loop).

**Flutter** — Flutter’s Dart widget tree and rendering engine share an implementation across mobile, desktop, and web, with Cupertino and Material widgets and native interop where needed. Its separate GenUI SDK adds widget catalogs and an A2UI adapter around `SurfaceController`, but Flutter documents that package as alpha. I’d pick Flutter if one shared client codebase mattered most, then pin and test the generative layer and keep authorization outside it. [Flutter repository](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) · [GenUI SDK architecture](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui/components).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — `MaterialTheme` propagates color, type, and shape to Kotlin composables, with dynamic color and a fallback on older Android versions. It’s a direct choice for Android-native presentation. AppFunctions is a separate, experimental route for exposing tools to authorized callers; neither Material styling nor Compose alone provides a shared web action contract. I’d keep domain operations independent of AppFunctions and validate the integration on supported devices before relying on it. [Material 3 in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) · [AppFunctions](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions).

reviews.pullQuote: With Ouro UI, an agent can prepare a sharing action, but it can’t relabel the button or remove the confirmation.
reviews.testimonial: I’d choose Ouro UI because I want the button a person sees and the tool an agent calls to agree about what will happen. Its one action model generates both from a declaration, and `compare-mcp` checks what the running server actually advertises. The `ActionButton` validator rejects a generated card that disguises “Share recipe” as “Add to list.” Flutter would let me maintain one UI implementation across platforms; with Ouro, I’d take on separate native kits and test the Android flow on hardware before shipping.
reviews.evaluations:
**A2UI** — My pick for a portable *wire format*. Its [SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/) negotiate catalogs and apply updates by component ID, so changing one part of a form needn’t cost the user focus in another. Its [function rules](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/) distinguish remote callers from functions requiring a user gesture. A gesture alone doesn’t establish that a button accurately describes the action. I’d pair A2UI with trusted action labels and reviewed confirmation screens, and negotiate versions: the documented Compose renderer supports 0.9.1, not all the 1.0 rules.

**Flutter** — A [single Dart widget implementation](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) can serve mobile, desktop and web, with Material and Cupertino controls and platform channels for OS integration. The [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui) goes beyond chat: it builds from a widget catalog and feeds interaction state back to the agent, though the package is marked alpha. I’d prefer Flutter if sharing the whole screen implementation were paramount; I’d still define callable business operations and approval rules independently of widget state.

**Radix UI** — `asChild` can put both dialog and tooltip behavior on one real button rather than nesting interactive elements. The [composition guide](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition) also identifies exactly how a custom trigger can break: drop its ref or props, or replace it with a non-focusable element. I’d use Radix for the web controls, test the composed triggers with a keyboard, and expose the underlying actions separately rather than ask an agent to operate dialogs.

**json-render** — `defineCatalog` describes components and actions, `defineRegistry` binds them to implementations, and SpecStream progressively applies model output. The [renderer examples](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render) cover React Native as well as web, even PDF and terminal output. That breadth is excellent for a reporting product. For an editable or consequential workflow, I’d constrain the relationship between label and action as well as their individual types: the example Button accepts both as strings. I’d also authorize the handler regardless of whether a press or a state watcher triggered it.

**Ouro UI** — The deciding evidence was a [validator test](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/a8d6c3076a342bfcede72d874de9354dcaa4e2fa/test/composed.test.mts) that changes a share button’s label, removes its confirmation, and tries to supply input to a person-only order; each change is rejected. The [action generator](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) also checks generated files and the live MCP tool list for drift. These checks complement, rather than replace, authorization in the handlers. The [platform matrix](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md) distinguishes native tree rendering on all four targets from A2UI ingestion on web and Apple. I’d pilot on actual devices: the [Android kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) documents eight standalone controls and emulator-only testing; the [Windows kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) has not verified agent discovery on a Windows client.

**MCP Apps** — The [specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) links a tool to a `ui://` HTML resource; a sandboxed iframe communicates with the host over JSON-RPC. I’d use that to deliver an interactive chart across compatible chat clients without rebuilding it for each one. The portable artifact is a web view, not a native widget tree, and extension support is negotiated. I’d keep the tool useful without the view and provide a native renderer where host controls matter.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) gives me adaptive controls and model-driven views; the [HIG](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines) guides choices such as layout and input conventions. [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) makes this a serious agent-facing option too: named actions and entities become discoverable to Siri and Shortcuts without anyone navigating a screen. I’d choose it directly for Apple-only delivery. For the broader brief, I want the same operation defined for a web tool and Android client without keeping three declarations in sync.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [UI library](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) supplies Radix-based React components and Tailwind 4 tokens matched to ChatGPT. That solves a concrete problem: a reservation card can look and behave like part of the host. The [integration guide](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/chatgpt-ui/) separates those optional components from the MCP Apps bridge and recommends keeping tools usable without UI. I’d follow that separation for ChatGPT distribution, not adopt this host’s styling as the foundation for standalone native screens.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The [architecture](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum/blob/main/rfcs/2019-v3-architecture.md) separates platform-independent state, interaction hooks and themed components. That lets me keep keyboard, focus and internationalization behavior when replacing the visual design, a strong reason to use it for complex web inputs. Reusable selection state, however, doesn’t tell an agent what selecting a record permits it to do. I’d put these controls behind a web renderer and bind them to the same domain actions as the native views.

**Tamagui** — Its [optional compiler](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/compiler-install) can flatten styled JSX into DOM and CSS on web or plain React Native views on mobile. That’s a practical way for one team to share screens, themes and variants without requiring every styling abstraction to survive at runtime. I’d choose it for a React/React Native product with an existing tool API. For this brief I’d have to supply the connection from that API to the controls, including when a person must confirm.

**AI Elements** — I’d use its presentation patterns for a conversation: Message Scroller keeps the reader’s place, Trace groups tool activity, and Confirmation gives a person an approval affordance. The original [repository](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces its move; the [shadcn migration guide](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements) explains that existing copies still work and identifies patterns without replacements. For new work I’d use the successor patterns. Drawing a confirmation prompt is useful, but the backend must refuse execution without approval, including from clients that don’t display chat.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — The closest competitor on shared business operations. Its [action layer](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) routes UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI calls through the same server implementation, validation, access checks and audit trail. I’d prefer that design for a TypeScript workspace where the hard problem is synchronizing people and agents around shared records. For native delivery I favor Ouro’s generated system actions and checked button labels; I’d otherwise budget for binding native controls to Builder’s excellent backend contract.

**Vercel UI SDK** — This beta goes beyond helping agents *write* components. Its [browser bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/reference) exposes `snapshot`, `query` and `act`; an `allow` callback can refuse a resolved action, and a marked confirmation fails without approval. The [behavior core](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui) serves five web adapters. I’d use it when the task really is editing what’s on the page. An off-page component has no available actions, though, so I’d give durable operations their own API rather than make them depend on a mounted control.

**CopilotKit** — AG-UI carries events between an existing agent and the frontend, with shared state, A2UI and MCP Apps support in the [stack](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit). Its [human-in-the-loop guide](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/human-in-the-loop) makes an important distinction: the model chooses whether to ask via `useHumanInTheLoop`, whereas backend code can require a pause via an interrupt. I’d choose it for a collaborative copilot, use an enforced checkpoint for mandatory approval, and verify backend support: the guide notes interrupts are temporarily unavailable on the Built-in Agent. I’d still want a common action definition for entry points outside the conversation.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Android’s [MaterialTheme](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) propagates color, typography and shape to composables and can adapt colors to the user’s wallpaper. [AppFunctions](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions) lets authorized callers discover and execute app operations on-device; Google marks the API experimental. I’d use both for an Android-first product and test discovery on the supported OS versions. Neither Android theming nor OS registration is a shared declaration for my web and Apple clients.

**Base UI** — Its [composition contract](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition) specifies how `render` merges classes, styles, handlers and refs onto one element, including which handler can stop subsequent ones. That precision matters when a branded toolbar button also opens a menu. I’d choose it for a custom React design system. I wouldn’t use merged click-handler order as a business permission check; native and agent callers need an operation that enforces the rule independently of the React tree.

**Fluent UI** — The [web project](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) offers distinct React v9, v8 and Web Component implementations, including a gradual migration path for Office-style apps. The separate [React Native library](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-react-native) explicitly calls its targets alpha and documents per-control platform differences. I’d use Fluent where Microsoft product consistency matters, but verify the required controls on each device rather than assume visual parity implies behavioral parity. I’d keep tool definitions shared outside those component packages.

**MUI** — [Material UI](https://github.com/mui/material-ui) pairs a comprehensive React implementation of Material Design with MUI X for complex controls, a persuasive starting point for a data-heavy web console. Its [MCP server](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/) supplies official documentation and examples to coding assistants; that is different from exposing the console’s own operations to an end-user agent. I’d reuse MUI on web and put record selection and mutation behind a typed service shared with native clients.

**Chakra UI** — Its [React component system](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui) offers accessible styled controls, and the [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) let a coding agent look up actual component props, examples and theme tokens rather than guess. That’s a useful authoring advantage, not a runtime contract for actions in the finished app. I’d use Chakra to implement web views for a team already using it, with a separate action catalog for agent and native access.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [registry](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry) distributes source files, including hooks, pages and rules, and isn’t restricted to React. That gives a team ownership of its controls and gives coding agents inspectable examples. It also means two applications can install the same button and later change what it does independently. I’d use the registry for distribution, then share action schemas and run conformance checks on the installed implementations rather than treat common source ancestry as a runtime guarantee.
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

reviews.pullQuote: I would choose Ouro UI for its shared action declarations, consent-aware composed interfaces, and native platform renderers—while budgeting for substantial platform-parity work.
reviews.testimonial: I would choose Ouro UI because its one action model connects human controls and agent tools, while ComposedSurface validates generated trees against an application catalog. I also value the consent classes and ax-xray checks: they make action policy and agent-facing behavior explicit rather than leaving them entirely to each screen. Compared with A2UI, however, Ouro has a narrower composed catalog and uneven native implementations; Android and Windows do not directly read A2UI messages. I would require real-device testing, server-side authorization, and platform-specific acceptance tests before relying on it in production.
reviews.evaluations:
**React Aria and React Spectrum** — React Aria separates unstyled accessibility behavior from React Stately state; Spectrum supplies Adobe-styled components. Its screen-reader, keyboard and internationalization work is excellent, but the UI layer targets the web rather than providing a shared native-and-agent action model. I would pair it with native kits and an explicit action layer for a web-first product. [Source](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/accessibility.html).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — SwiftUI composes views, state and event handlers into adaptive Apple-native interfaces; the HIG supplies platform design guidance. This is a strong Apple choice, but it does not itself cover Android or web. Separate platform implementations and an interoperable action contract would address that scope. [Source](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui).

**json-render** — Zod catalogs constrain generated specs, registries map names to implementations, and SpecStream progressively applies JSON patches. It has web and React Native renderers plus MCP Apps integration, making it a strong alternative for shared generated UI; I prefer Ouro's explicit action consent classes and platform-native kits. Application handlers still need authorization and validation, and separate native registries and policy enforcement would be needed for comparable coverage. [Source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md).

**Ouro UI** — Core generates human and agent surfaces from action declarations, while catalog-validated composed trees bind fields and actions to platform renderers. I would choose it for that combination, but its own documentation lists just eight Android and Windows kit controls versus 125 on web; Android has only emulator testing, and neither Android nor Windows reads A2UI messages directly. Real-device and Windows-client testing, more native controls, and app-level authorization and confirmation integration are prerequisites for my deployment. [Android limitations](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md); [composed UI](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md).

**Base UI** — Its unstyled React primitives expose composable parts, including portal, positioning and popup behavior, while leaving styling to the application. This is a good foundation for a custom accessible web system, but native rendering and product action policy would need separate layers. A shared action service and native implementations would address those needs. [Source](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start).

**MCP Apps** — The extension links an MCP tool to a `ui://` HTML resource rendered in a sandboxed iframe, with bidirectional host communication. It is valuable distribution infrastructure for interactive tool results, but host support varies and the specified UI resource is HTML rather than a native cross-platform design system. I would use it alongside a toolkit with native renderers and application-level permissions. [Specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx).

**Vercel UI SDK** — Framework-neutral behaviors and `definePrimitive` separate interaction logic from React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components adapters; its agent bridge exposes component state and actions with an `allow` callback and WebMCP integration. That is more than coding-agent documentation, but the SDK is beta and its documented adapters are web-oriented. Native adapters and independently enforced backend authorization would make it a closer fit. [Source](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Styled React components built on Radix, Tailwind 4 tokens and responsive utilities make it a practical way to match ChatGPT app visuals. It is a presentation library rather than a cross-platform action and consent architecture; pair it with MCP Apps and separate native clients when ChatGPT distribution is the priority. [Source](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — `MaterialTheme` supplies color, typography and shape to native Compose components, including dynamic color; Android also documents an A2UI Compose renderer and Material 3 catalog. This is a compelling Android-native stack, but the selected Compose implementation does not by itself deliver the corresponding Apple and web implementations. I would combine it with those clients and a shared action contract. [Material 3](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3); [A2UI renderer](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/agentic).

**Fluent UI** — Fluent spans React, Web Components and separate Apple, Android and Windows libraries, so it has a broader native footprint than the web repository alone suggests. Its platform libraries and their component migration stages still require coordination, and the design system does not itself establish a single human/agent action contract. A shared action layer would address the latter. [Source](https://fluent2.microsoft.design/get-started/develop).

**CopilotKit** — AG-UI streams agent events to frontend SDKs, with shared state, frontend tools, human approval and generative UI; its A2UI integration supports both fixed and dynamically generated schemas. I would consider it for an agent-centric application, but it is an agent-experience stack rather than a complete native visual system. Pairing it with platform design kits and validating approval behavior per tool would close the practical gap. [Source](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit).

**Tamagui** — Universal React/React Native components share typed tokens and styles; its optional compiler extracts atomic CSS on web and flattens native component trees. It offers substantially more implementation reuse than Ouro, but an agent action, authorization and consent layer remains an application concern. I would add one when shared React code is the overriding priority. [Source](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction).

**MUI** — Material UI provides a broad, customizable React component library with MUI X for more complex controls. Its documentation identifies its Material implementation as Material Design 2, not the Material 3 Compose implementation, and it does not supply native clients through this library. Native kits and an agent-facing action service would be needed for this brief. [Source](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — `defineAction` exposes the same server implementation to React, agents, HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI, with common validation and access checks; `needsApproval` can pause agent execution. This is a serious alternative for shared operations, but its documented primary UI is a React application framework rather than Ouro's separate native design kits. I would pair it with native UI systems and carefully configure its permissive action-exposure defaults. [Actions](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview/); [access controls](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-access-control/).

**Radix UI** — Low-level web primitives provide ARIA roles, keyboard navigation and focus management while allowing application-defined styling. They are an excellent accessible substrate, but the application must supply the design system, native implementations and agent action policy. Those layers would make Radix more appropriate for this cross-platform brief. [Source](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/accessibility).

**Chakra UI** — Chakra supplies accessible React web components and theme tokens; its MCP server helps coding agents discover components, props and examples. That MCP server assists development rather than automatically exposing an application's business actions to its users' agents. I would add a separate action service and native UI kits for the requested scope. [Source](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server.mdx).

**AI Elements** — Copy-in React patterns cover conversations, messages, reasoning and other AI-facing presentation, but they are not a native platform system or an action authorization layer. The repository announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 in favor of shadcn/ui's version; new projects should assess that migration path and supply their own runtime and native interfaces. [Source](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements).

**shadcn/ui** — Its registry and CLI distribute editable component source rather than a conventional packaged component library, and its AI Elements patterns include confirmation and tool displays. This is attractive for ownership and agent-assisted editing, but copied code brings update maintenance and does not itself unify native actions or enforce approvals. A versioning process and a shared action layer would address those trade-offs. [Source](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs).

**A2UI** — The protocol separates streamed component updates from a bound data model, with catalog validation and renderers for web, Flutter and SwiftUI; Android's Compose renderer currently documents v0.9.1 while v1.0 support is in progress. It is my strongest interoperability alternative and offers broader renderer choices than Ouro, but I would still implement application authorization and consent policy around its actions. Standardizing those policies and testing protocol-version parity across clients would make it especially compelling. [SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/); [client integration](https://a2ui.org/guides/client-integration/).

**Flutter** — Flutter draws Material and Cupertino widgets from a shared Dart codebase across mobile, web and desktop, and its GenUI SDK can connect generated surfaces to A2UI. That offers more code reuse than Ouro, but Flutter draws its own widgets rather than using each platform's native UI toolkit, and the documented `genui` package is alpha. I would choose it when single-codebase consistency matters more, with platform accessibility testing and a separate action-permission layer. [Flutter](https://github.com/flutter/flutter); [GenUI](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui/get-started.md).

reviews.evaluations:
**Ouro UI** — Splits interface design into [Ouro HX](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui) for human screens (125 copy-in React 19 + Base UI + Tailwind CSS v4 components on web, 20 SwiftUI views in `OuroHX` on Apple, and 8-control WinUI 3 and Jetpack Compose kits) and [Ouro AX](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax.md) for agent surfaces (`ax-command`, `ax-outcome`, `ax-wait`, `ax-claims`, and external conformance runners `ax-xray` and `ouro-ax-xray`). Its unifying architectural move is a single `defineAction` declaration with structural consent classes (`read`, `write`, `consequential`, `person-only`) that generates CLI commands, MCP/WebMCP tools, web controls, Apple App Intents, SwiftUI buttons, Windows App Actions, and Android AppFunctions while refusing agent access to person-only doors, paired with [Composed UI](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md) (`ComposedSurface`, `OuroMcpApp`, `A2UISurface`) for schema-validated, incrementally updatable native cards that speak both MCP Apps and A2UI. The main trade-off is platform maturity asymmetry and deliberate rejection of a shared cross-platform runtime: while web and [Apple v1.2.0](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/apple.md) are well-developed, [Android v0.3.0](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) and [Windows v0.3.0](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) ship only 8 components each, lack direct A2UI message adapters, and rely on emulator/Windows Server CI rather than physical Android devices or Windows 11 client validation. Expanding component coverage on Android and Windows, landing Android `PendingIntent` consequential confirmation and physical-device testing, and publishing to Maven Central and nuget.org would close those observed gaps.

**AI Elements** — Provides a registry of copy-in React components built on shadcn/ui, Tailwind CSS, and the Vercel AI SDK—covering [49 specialized AI UI files](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements/tree/main/packages/elements/src) such as `conversation`, `message`, `reasoning`, `chain-of-thought`, `confirmation`, `plan`, `tool`, `sandbox`, and `terminal`. Architecturally, it solves human-side rendering of agent traces and chat turns inside Next.js/React web apps, but its [README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) explicitly announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 in favor of upstream `shadcn/ui` AI Elements. Even setting aside deprecation, it is web/React-DOM only (requiring CSS Variables Tailwind mode) and offers no native mobile/desktop kits, no runtime generative UI catalog validator, and no agent-callable tool/CLI surface; adopting its successor inside `shadcn/ui` addresses the deprecation, though cross-platform and agent-surface gaps remain.

**Radix UI** — Pioneered accessible, unstyled React compound components (`Root`, `Trigger`, `Portal`, `Content`) with DOM composition via `Slot`/`asChild`, roving focus, `DismissableLayer`, and ARIA wiring across [its React primitives](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives/tree/main/packages/react). While [Radix Primitives](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives) remains a rock-solid accessibility layer beneath many web design systems, it is strictly bound to `react-dom` without native iOS, Android, or desktop primitives, provides no visual token system of its own, and includes no primitives for agent action schemas, tool surfaces, or runtime composed UI. Pairing Radix with a separate native stack and an agent protocol layer would be required to use it here, and even on the web, much of the ecosystem (including shadcn/ui and Ouro HX) now favors Base UI's `render`-prop model.

**Flutter** — Compiles Dart to native ARM/x64 machine code and WebAssembly/JS while rendering its own widget tree (Material and Cupertino catalogs) through the hardware-accelerated Impeller and Skia engines, as documented in the [Flutter repository](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) and [engineering wiki](https://github.com/flutter/flutter/blob/main/docs/README.md). That custom canvas architecture gives pixel-identical cross-platform reach across iOS, Android, web, Windows, macOS, and Linux—and pairs with `a2ui_flutter` for streamed generative UI—but trades away native DOM semantics on the web and true platform-native control feel on desktop/mobile, while providing no built-in unified action/consent model or MCP/CLI agent interface toolkit. First-class DOM/native control interop without canvas trade-offs plus an integrated agent action and conformance layer would address my main reservations.

**Vercel UI SDK** — Separates interaction mechanics (`createPopup`, `createSelection`, `createTypeahead`, `createFocusRecovery`, `createVirtualizer`, `createLasso`, `createGridFocus`) into a framework-agnostic kernel in [`@ui-sdk/core`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/blob/main/packages/core/src/index.ts) with thin `createParts` adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components, plus [51 headless component definitions](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/tree/main/packages/core/src/components) and an agent coding skill. As shown in the [UI SDK README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui), it is thoughtfully engineered for coding agents *authoring* complex web UIs, but it is in public beta, unstyled, DOM-exclusive (no native iOS/Android/Windows targets), and includes no runtime protocol for agents *using* the resulting interface via tools, actions, or validated UI trees. Shipping GA APIs, design tokens, native platform adapters, and runtime agent action bindings would make it viable for full cross-platform human-and-agent apps.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Delivers Tailwind CSS v4 design tokens and [29 React 18/19 components](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/tree/main/src/components) (`Alert`, `Badge`, `Button`, `CodeBlock`, `DatePicker`, `Markdown`, `Menu`, `Popover`, `Select`, `ShimmerText`, etc.) built over Radix primitives for embedded ChatGPT experiences via the [Apps SDK UI package](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui). It excels at lightweight visual consistency inside ChatGPT web views, but its component surface is intentionally compact and scoped to React/DOM iframes rather than standalone multi-platform web and native applications, and it leaves MCP/tool definitions and consent mechanics to external SDK layers. Broadening the component catalog for full standalone apps and adding native mobile/desktop kits and action schemas would be necessary to choose it as a primary cross-platform system.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Provides Apple's declarative `View` and `Scene` hierarchy, reactive state flow, Liquid Glass materials, accessibility modifiers, and deep OS integration across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and visionOS ([SwiftUI documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)), backed by comprehensive platform ergonomics in the [Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines). Paired with Apple's App Intents framework, it offers superb native quality for both people and system agents on Apple hardware, but it is strictly proprietary to Apple OSes with zero web, Android, or Windows rendering path. Only an official cross-platform/web SwiftUI runtime and cross-OS agent action target—which Apple does not provide—would let it serve as a single cross-platform toolkit.

**CopilotKit** — Acts as an open-source full-stack agentic UI orchestration layer built around the **AG-UI 1.0** event-streaming protocol, connecting 14+ agent frameworks to React, Angular, Vue, React Native, and Channels JSX (rendering native Slack Block Kit and Teams Adaptive Cards), as detailed in the [CopilotKit README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit). Its support for `useAgent` shared state, human-in-the-loop pauses, WebMCP, and three generative UI modes (controlled registered components, declarative A2UI 1.0, and sandboxed MCP Apps) makes it formidable middleware, yet it is a copilot/agent integration layer rather than a foundational design system for building an app's core human UI, and it lacks native SwiftUI, Compose, or WinUI kits and CLI/App Intents conformance tooling. Pairing it with a full multi-platform component system—or shipping first-party native kits and non-chat UI primitives—would address that gap.

**Tamagui** — Combines a universal typed style system (`@tamagui/core`), an optimizing static compiler (`@tamagui/static`) that flattens styled components into atomic CSS `div`s on web and hoisted `View` styles on React Native, and a cross-platform UI kit ([Tamagui README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui) and [workspace packages](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui/tree/main/code/packages)). It solves React Web + React Native code sharing with minimal runtime overhead, but it contains no agentic architecture whatsoever—no action/tool schema, no consent model, no generative UI validator, and no MCP or OS-intent integration—while relying on React Native rather than native desktop/mobile toolkits like SwiftUI or WinUI. Adding a validated declarative agent-surface spec and unified action/tool bindings would be required to serve agent users alongside human ones.

**shadcn/ui** — Defines an open-code component distribution model (`components.json` flat-file schema, CLI, namespaced registries, `shadcn` MCP server, and coding skills) whose [v4 documentation](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui/tree/main/apps/v4/content/docs) now includes built-in [AI Elements](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui/blob/main/apps/v4/content/docs/ai-elements/index.mdx) (`Chat`, `Message Scroller`, `Trace`, `Reasoning`, `Confirmation`, `Plan`, `Subagent`, `Tool`) across Base UI, Radix, and React Aria. Having source files in-repo makes coding agents remarkably effective at reading and customizing web UIs, which is why Ouro HX adopts shadcn's registry format and theme variables directly. However, [shadcn/ui](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui) itself remains React-DOM/web-only with no native iOS, Android, or Windows kits, no runtime schema-validated composed UI renderer, and no runtime agent surface (CLI/MCP/App Intents) for agents operating the live app; adding cross-platform native registries and a shared runtime action contract would bridge that gap.

**A2UI** — Establishes a security-first, streaming generative UI protocol and multi-language SDK (`a2ui-core` / `a2ui-agent-sdk` in Python, `@a2ui/web_core` and `@a2ui/agent` in TypeScript, `a2ui_core` in Dart) that maps validated JSON widget catalogs and data-model expressions to native renderers for Lit, Angular, React, Flutter, and SwiftUI ([A2UI README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui)). Expressing UI strictly as schema-validated data across trust boundaries without WebViews is an excellent design for remote agent-to-human cards, but A2UI covers only one direction of the problem: an agent streaming dynamic widgets to a human. It is not a complete human design system for authoring full applications, lacks an in-repo Jetpack Compose or WinUI renderer package today, and does not define agent-callable CLI/MCP/OS-intent surfaces or action consent tiers when an agent is the caller; pairing it with a full design system and bidirectional action model (as Ouro UI does via its A2UI adapter) addresses these limits.

**json-render** — Offers an expansive catalog-constrained generative UI framework (`defineCatalog` with Zod schemas, `defineRegistry`, progressive `SpecStream` patching, and `$state`/`$cond`/`$template`/`watch` reactive expressions) spanning [30 packages](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render) including React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, 36 pre-built shadcn components, React Native, Next.js/TanStack Start full-app specs, Ink terminal UIs, Remotion video, PDF, Email, Three.js, Chat SDK cards, and MCP Apps. Its breadth of output targets and drop-in devtools are unmatched among JSON UI renderers, yet it remains a Labs-stage spec-to-UI renderer (`0.x`) rather than a cohesive human design system, targets mobile only via React Native rather than native SwiftUI/Compose/WinUI, and lacks first-class consent classes (`consequential` vs. `person-only`) or external agent-surface conformance checks. Adding unified bidirectional action/consent semantics across CLI/MCP/OS intents and native mobile/desktop renderers would address those trade-offs.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Implements Google's Material You and Material 3 Expressive system (`MaterialTheme` color tonal palettes, dynamic wallpaper colors, typography, shapes, adaptive window size classes, and semantics trees) alongside Glance widgets, Remote Compose, and documented A2UI agentic catalog rendering on Android ([Material 3 in Compose docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). Its declarative Kotlin state hoisting, accessibility semantics, and emerging Android AppFunctions/A2UI hooks make it first-rate for Android devices, foldables, Wear OS, and XR. However, Google's M3 Compose stack is Android-centric (and even with JetBrains Compose Multiplatform, web and iOS rely on Skia canvas rendering rather than native DOM/UIKit controls, while AppFunctions remain Android-specific), so it cannot serve as a native-feeling web + multi-OS toolkit with a cross-platform agent action layer on its own.

**Base UI** — Built by creators of Radix, Floating UI, and Material UI, [Base UI](https://github.com/mui/base-ui) ships [over 35 unstyled, accessible React components](https://github.com/mui/base-ui/tree/main/packages/react/src) (`Dialog`, `Drawer`, `Combobox`, `Autocomplete`, `Menu`, `Menubar`, `NumberField`, `OtpField`, `Select`, `Toast`, `Toolbar`, etc.) using clean `use-render` (`render` prop) composition and `merge-props` instead of fragile `cloneElement` slots. Its DOM ergonomics and accessibility rigor make it my favorite low-level React web primitive layer—indeed, Ouro HX and shadcn/ui v4 build directly on `@base-ui/react`—but Base UI intentionally stops at unstyled `react-dom` primitives. Because it provides no styling/token system, no native mobile or desktop components, and no agent tool, action, or generative UI layer, it is a foundational web dependency rather than a complete cross-platform human-and-agent design system.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Centers its TypeScript application framework on `defineAction` in `@agent-native/core`, exposing a single Zod-validated capability simultaneously to React (`useActionQuery`), agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, with thoughtful privacy controls (`persistInChatHistory: false`, `persistInBrowser: false`, and server-keyed opaque approvals), as documented in the [Agent-Native README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native) and [development guide](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md). While its shared-action philosophy closely parallels what mixed human/agent software needs, it is an opinionated full-stack app framework coupled to Node/Nitro and PostgreSQL/PGlite rather than a reusable design system or component toolkit, and its cross-platform reach relies on an Electron wrapper and an [Expo companion mobile app](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/mobile-app/README.md) (which currently hits Xcode 26.x / Expo SDK 57 JSI native compile blockers in hosted CI) instead of native platform UI kits and validated composed UI catalogs. Decoupling a portable multi-platform UI/token kit from the Nitro/Postgres server stack and stabilizing native mobile builds would address those constraints.

**Chakra UI** — Combines accessible state-machine primitives (`@ark-ui/react`) with an Emotion and recipe/token-based styled system (`@chakra-ui/react` v3.38, plus charts, CLI, Panda preset, and a `@chakra-ui/react-mcp` Cursor server) for building RSC-compatible React web apps ([Chakra UI README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui) and [`packages/react/package.json`](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui/blob/main/packages/react/package.json)). Its anatomy/slot recipes and MCP documentation server make web authoring productive for both developers and coding agents, but runtime `@emotion/react` peer dependencies bind it strictly to `react-dom` on the web with no native iOS, Android, or Windows rendering path, and it includes no runtime agent action, consent, or generative UI protocol. Native cross-platform primitives and runtime agent-surface tooling would be needed to contend here.

**Fluent UI** — Unifies Microsoft's web design language in `@fluentui/react-components` (v9), featuring `FluentProvider` design tokens, slot-based JSX composition, accessibility defaults, and zero-runtime/atomic Griffel CSS-in-JS alongside Web Components ([Fluent UI README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) and [`@fluentui/react-components` README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui/blob/master/packages/react-components/react-components/README.md)). While Fluent as a broader Microsoft brand has separate repositories for Windows/Apple/Android, this toolkit (`microsoft/fluentui`) is strictly web-focused (split across legacy React v8, converged React v9, and beta Web Components v3) and offers no cross-platform code/spec sharing, generative UI catalog, or agent action/MCP layer. Consolidating cross-platform token/claim parity with native kits and adding agent action and composed-UI primitives would address why I passed on it.

**MCP Apps** — Standardizes interactive UI delivery over the Model Context Protocol (`io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`, [SEP-1865](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)) by linking tools to `ui://` HTML resources (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`) rendered inside sandboxed iframes with declarative CSP/permission metadata and bidirectional JSON-RPC via `@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps` (`App`, `PostMessageTransport`, `AppBridge`), as detailed in the [MCP Apps repository](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps). It is an essential interoperability transport across Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose, and Postman, but it is a sandboxed HTML container protocol rather than a design system or component library, ships no production host implementation beyond `examples/basic-host`, and relies on web iframes that cannot deliver native platform controls, haptics, or OS-level accessibility outside a WebView. Using MCP Apps as a wire transport *underneath* a native-capable kit like Ouro UI captures its ecosystem reach without accepting iframe-only UX everywhere.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Pairs industry-leading WAI-ARIA, pointer/touch/keyboard, and 30+ locale internationalization hooks (`react-aria`, `react-stately`, `react-aria-components`) with Adobe's Spectrum and Spectrum 2 (`@react-spectrum/s2`) design system ([React Spectrum README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)), and now includes [`@react-spectrum/ai`](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum/tree/main/packages/@react-spectrum/ai/src) (`Chat`, `PromptField`, `AIButton`, `MessageSource`, `ResponseStatus`, `useVoiceInput`) plus [MCP servers for React Aria and S2](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum/tree/main/packages/dev/mcp). Its accessibility engineering and state separation (`react-stately`) are exceptional on the web, yet the rendering layer remains DOM-only (while `react-stately` hooks are platform-agnostic, no official SwiftUI, Compose, or React Native UI kits ship in the repo) and `@react-spectrum/ai` covers human-side chat widgets rather than bidirectional agent tools, CLI/App Intents surfaces, or runtime composed-UI validation. Official native platform renderers and a shared action/consent layer would make it a top cross-platform contender.

**MUI** — Delivers a battle-tested React implementation of Material Design (`@mui/material`), complemented by `MUI X` data-heavy components and build-time `pigment-css-react` alongside Emotion/styled-components engines ([Material UI README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui) and [packages directory](https://github.com/mui/material-ui/tree/master/packages)). Despite massive enterprise maturity for human-operated React web dashboards, MUI remains locked to `react-dom` on the web (with its core README still anchored in Material Design 2 roots alongside ongoing styling-engine transitions), provides no native mobile or desktop UI kits, and offers no architecture for runtime agent tool surfaces, consent boundaries, or schema-validated generative UI. Adding cross-platform native targets and a first-class agent action/generative-UI contract would be required to fit this brief.
reviews.pullQuote: Unifying human screens, agent tools, and native Composed UI around one consent-aware action model, Ouro UI treats people and agents as equal peers.
reviews.testimonial: I would choose Ouro UI because it designs the human screen and the agent surface from a single contract instead of bolting agent glue onto a web-only widget kit. With Ouro HX and Ouro AX backed by one defineAction declaration, a single capability generates a Base UI web control, SwiftUI button, CLI command, MCP tool, and App Intent with enforced consent classes—while ComposedSurface renders agent-composed trees natively across web, Apple, Windows, and Android. Built-in verification via ax-xray and ouro-check turns both agent ergonomics and visual accessibility into CI-enforced claims rather than wishful prompts.
