reviews.evaluations:
**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A lightweight React 18/19 and Tailwind 4 design system built on Radix primitives for rendering consistent experiences inside ChatGPT via the Apps SDK ([OpenAI Apps SDK UI README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). Its trade-off is narrow scope: it is web-only, React-only, and tied to ChatGPT's Apps SDK host environment, offering neither native mobile/desktop kits nor general-purpose agent-facing interfaces (CLI, MCP servers, or OS intents). Supporting native platform targets and host-agnostic agent action layers would be required for broader use.

**Radix UI** — Unstyled, accessible React primitives for building web design systems ([Radix Primitives README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). While it excels at WAI-ARIA compliance and keyboard/focus behavior on the web, it provides no native mobile or desktop implementations and no agent-facing protocol, action model, or generative UI layer. You would have to pair it with separate native kits and build the entire agent-interface layer yourself.

**Tamagui** — A universal styling system (`@tamagui/core`), optimizing compiler (`@tamagui/static`), and UI kit (`tamagui`) for sharing code across React on the web and React Native on mobile ([Tamagui README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). Its compile-time flattening gives strong cross-platform performance, but it is strictly a human-facing UI layer with no built-in agent action model, consent enforcement, or generative UI protocol. Addressing that gap would require layering a framework like CopilotKit or A2UI on top.

**MCP Apps** — An extension to the Model Context Protocol (`@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps`) that lets MCP tools declare `ui://` HTML resources rendered in sandboxed iframes inside compliant chat hosts like Claude, ChatGPT, and VS Code ([MCP Apps README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)). It solves portable, bidirectional tool-to-UI communication inside chat clients, but it is inherently iframe/web-based rather than a native cross-platform design system for standalone apps. Native host renderers or integration with native UI kits would be needed outside chat iframes.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — A TypeScript framework (`@agent-native/core`) where capabilities are declared once via `defineAction` and exposed simultaneously to React (`useActionQuery`), agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, backed by shared data and application state ([Agent-Native README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)). Its architecture aligns closely with dual human/agent interfaces, but it targets TypeScript/React web apps on Nitro-compatible servers and lacks native iOS, Android, or Windows UI kits. Adding native platform SDKs and a cross-platform component catalog would close that gap.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Adobe's ecosystem comprising React Spectrum (Adobe's design system in React), React Aria (unstyled accessible web components and hooks), and React Stately (cross-platform state hooks) ([React Spectrum README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). Although React Stately's state hooks are platform-agnostic, React Aria and React Spectrum are web-only React implementations and provide no agent-facing action declarations, generative UI protocol, or native mobile/desktop component kits.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's Fluent UI Web repository housing React v9, React v8, and Web Components (`@fluentui/web-components`) with Griffel styling and accessibility defaults ([Fluent UI README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). This repository targets web browsers exclusively and does not include native Apple/Android/Windows UI kits or an agent-surface layer (CLI, MCP, or generative UI). Cross-platform native and agentic support would require separate platform toolkits and an external agent protocol.

**Chakra UI** — An accessible React component system (`@chakra-ui/react` with `@emotion/react`) designed for rapid web development and Next.js RSC ([Chakra UI README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). While it ships a coding-agent MCP server (`@chakra-ui/react-mcp`) for developer assistance, it offers no runtime agent-user interface protocol, no shared action/consent model, and no native mobile or desktop platform support.

**MUI** — A comprehensive React implementation of Google's Material Design system (`@mui/material`), extended by MUI X for advanced data components ([Material UI README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). It is battle-tested for web applications, but it is web-only and lacks native iOS/Android/Windows kits as well as any built-in agent-facing interface, action model, or generative UI runtime.

**Ouro UI** — A complete dual-audience system pairing **Ouro HX** (human-facing native kits) with **Ouro AX** (agent-facing CLI, HTTP, MCP, App Intents, and AppFunctions) from a single `defineAction` declaration with built-in consent classes and CI-enforced X-ray checks (`ax-xray`, `ouro-ax-xray`) ([Ouro UI README](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui)). Its **Composed UI** (`ComposedSurface`, `OuroMcpApp`, `OuroComposedSurface`) also renders agent-composed trees natively and speaks both MCP Apps and A2UI ([Composed UI guide](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/)). The concrete trade-off is uneven platform maturity: Web ships 125 components and Apple ships 20 (v1.2.0, source-stable 1.0+), whereas Windows (v0.3.0, WinUI 3) and Android (v0.3.0, Jetpack Compose) ship only 8 components each; Android is tested on emulators only using experimental `compileSdk 37` AppFunctions without `PendingIntent` confirmation wired yet ([Android platform docs](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md)), and Windows CI runs on Windows Server without NuGet.org publishing yet ([Windows platform docs](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md)). Expanding the Windows and Android component catalogs and testing on physical hardware would resolve those gaps.

**CopilotKit** — An open-source agentic product stack supporting chat, generative UI (AG-UI tool calls, A2UI 1.0, and MCP Apps), shared state, and human-in-the-loop across React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack, and Microsoft Teams ([CopilotKit README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). It is strong for embedding agents into existing apps, but it is an orchestration and chat/copilot runtime rather than a unified native design system—mobile relies on React Native rather than native SwiftUI/Compose kits, and it does not generate CLI or OS-level App Intents from a single action schema.

**A2UI** — Google's open-source generative UI protocol and multi-language SDK stack (Core, Agent, and Renderer SDKs) that lets agents stream schema-validated UI descriptions to native renderers in Flutter (`a2ui_flutter`), React (`@a2ui/react`), Lit, Angular, SwiftUI (`A2UISwiftUI`), and Jetpack Compose (`androidx.a2ui.compose` / `material3-a2ui`) ([A2UI SDKs docs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). Its cross-platform native renderer coverage is its biggest strength, but A2UI is a generative UI wire protocol rather than a full human-authored design system for the rest of an app, and it lacks a unified action generator for CLI/MCP/App Intents with automated X-ray conformance checks ([A2UI README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui)).

**json-render** — Vercel Labs' generative UI framework (`@json-render/core`) where developers define Zod-typed component catalogs and registries, and AI generates progressive JSON specs rendered across React (`@json-render/shadcn`), Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, Remotion, PDF, Email, Ink, Three.js, and MCP Apps ([json-render README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). It offers remarkable output-target breadth, but native mobile relies on React Native (no SwiftUI, WinUI 3, or Jetpack Compose kits) and it focuses on constrained UI generation rather than generating CLI/OS-intent agent doors or verifying agent surfaces.

**Vercel UI SDK** — A beta library of headless interaction behaviors (`@ui-sdk/core`—focus recovery, popups, selection, typeahead, ARIA) with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components, paired with an agent skill so coding agents can author primitives ([Vercel UI SDK README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)). It is a promising behavior layer for agent-assisted web development, but it is web-only (no native iOS, Android, or Windows support) and provides no runtime agent-facing interface layer.

**Flutter** — Google's cross-platform UI toolkit compiling Dart to native ARM code, WebAssembly, and desktop via Skia/Impeller ([Flutter README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). It delivers consistent cross-platform human UIs from one codebase and pairs well with `a2ui_flutter` for generative UI, but out of the box it provides no agent-facing action model, MCP/CLI generation, or OS intent integration, and its non-native widget rendering trades away platform-native look and feel.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Android's declarative UI toolkit and Material Design 3 theming/component system (`androidx.compose.material3`) with dynamic color, typography, shapes, and adaptive layouts ([Material 3 in Compose docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). While Compose Multiplatform extends Compose beyond Android and `material3-a2ui` enables A2UI rendering on Android, Material 3 Compose itself is primarily an Android human-UI toolkit without a cross-platform Windows/Apple native-feel story or a unified cross-platform agent-surface generator.

**shadcn/ui** — A copy-in React component registry built on Tailwind CSS and unstyled primitives, designed for teams to own and customize their component code ([shadcn/ui README](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui)). It is an excellent web component foundation (and the base for Ouro HX on web and AI Elements' migration), but it is web-only and does not provide native mobile/desktop kits or runtime agent-interface primitives on its own.

**AI Elements** — A Vercel component library built on shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS for AI chat interfaces (conversations, messages, reasoning displays, code blocks) in Next.js apps ([AI Elements README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)). Notably, the repository carries a deprecation notice stating it is moving into shadcn/ui at the end of November 2026; even after migration, it remains a web-only React/Next.js chat UI kit without native platforms or agent-facing action/protocol layers.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Apple's declarative UI framework for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and visionOS ([SwiftUI documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). When paired with App Intents, it provides first-class human and agent integration on Apple hardware, but it is strictly locked to Apple platforms with no web, Android, or Windows story.

**Base UI** — An unstyled, accessible React component library for the web created by contributors from Radix, Floating UI, and Material UI ([Base UI README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)). Like Radix UI, it is a strong, accessible foundation for web UIs (and serves as the base layer for Ouro HX on web), but it is web-only and offers no native platform kits or agent-facing interface capabilities.

reviews.pullQuote: Ouro UI is the kit I would ship: one declared action, native screens for people, and a typed door for agents.
reviews.testimonial: I would build on Ouro UI. defineAction is the piece I do not want to reimplement: one declaration becomes the control a person presses and the MCP tool, App Intent, App Action, or AppFunction an agent calls, and the composed tree’s validator refuses a card that relabels a button or loosens its consent. ComposedSurface then draws that same tree in React, SwiftUI, WinUI 3, and Compose. I nearly picked A2UI instead, because its v1.0 protocol already has official Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose renderers, while Ouro’s Windows and Android kits are still v0.3.0 and will not read A2UI messages. I would rather own the action and consent model and speak A2UI where a host already requires it.
reviews.evaluations:
**Ouro UI** — This is the toolkit I would use. Core’s `defineAction` is the source of truth: a generator writes the person’s control and the agent doors (CLI, MCP, WebMCP, App Intent, Windows App Actions, Android AppFunctions), and a CI check fails if generated files drift. The composed tree is validated data, not HTML: `ActionButton` labels and consent classes come from the declaration, a consequential action confirms on a sheet, and a person-only action is a handoff that answers agents with a typed refusal. React `ComposedSurface`, SwiftUI `ComposedSurface`, WinUI `OuroComposedSurface`, and Compose `OuroComposedSurface` draw that tree; MCP Apps and A2UI are adapters into it, not the model. The objection I actually have is maturity, not architecture. Windows and Android are v0.3.0, with eight specified HX components and several composed nodes drawn from tokens; Android is emulator-only; neither kit reads A2UI messages; there is no Flutter kit, by an explicit decision. Device-tested Android, a Windows 11 check that the Agent Registry lists the doors, and A2UI readers on those two kits would answer that. Sources: [composed UI](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/), [Android kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-android), [Windows kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-windows), [native-kits decision](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/5f520a112feb806aa51a8e8bf6a716acdcdf6a54/docs/decisions/2026-11-17-native-kits-no-cross-platform.md).

**A2UI** — The strongest protocol I did not pick. v1.0 streams `createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, and bidirectional function calls; catalogs are JSON Schema; accessibility attributes map onto Flutter, web ARIA, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose. Official renderers are Flutter, React, Lit, Angular, SwiftUI, and Compose (`material3-a2ui`), with agent SDKs in TypeScript, Python, and Dart. It is a wire format and a basic catalog styled by the host theme, not a design system, and the SDK page lists no WinUI renderer and no person-only or consequential door shared with OS agent surfaces. I would emit it into hosts I do not own. A WinUI renderer plus consent constraints in the catalog would close the gap. Sources: [v1.0 specification](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/), [SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/).

**json-render** — A catalog-guardrailed generative UI framework: `defineCatalog` plus Zod props, `defineRegistry`, and a `Renderer` that streams a flat spec. The same catalog idea reaches React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, Remotion, PDF, email, Ink, and `@json-render/mcp`, which serves a single HTML file as an MCP App iframe. React Native’s standard set (Container, Row, Button, TextInput, Card, Modal) plus `StateStore` is a real mobile path. It is not SwiftUI, WinUI, or Compose, and a press dispatches a named action in the spec rather than an OS consent door. I would use it for a web product that also has to appear inside chat. A SwiftUI or Compose renderer bound to the same catalog schema would change the comparison. Sources: [repository README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render), [React Native renderer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/json-render/9301e64eb556f972c21eb471ae851603cab65e6b/packages/react-native/README.md), [MCP package](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/json-render/9301e64eb556f972c21eb471ae851603cab65e6b/packages/mcp/README.md).

**MCP Apps** — The embedding standard, not the product toolkit. SEP-1865, stable as of 2026-01-26, lets a server declare a `ui://` resource of type `text/html;profile=mcp-app`; the host renders it in a sandboxed iframe and the view talks JSON-RPC, with CSP fields for connect, resource, and frame origins. Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose, and Postman are named hosts. That is interactive UI inside someone else’s chat client. It does not draw a native screen, and the initial spec reserves non-HTML MIME types rather than defining them. I would implement this as a host format, which both Ouro and json-render already speak. A native content type would address the platform limit; it is not in the stable spec I read. Source: [SEP-1865](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/ea3e9d0e624a20bc1c51310292f09d9b8ed17161/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — The closest action architecture on the web. `defineAction` is scanned from `actions/` and mounted as the agent tool, React `useActionQuery` / `useActionMutation`, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, all through the same schema, access checks, and audit trail, over a shared Postgres database. Private results can set `persistInChatHistory: false`. It is a TypeScript application framework with its own chat, auth, and skills, not a design system, and the docs I read describe a React client. I found no SwiftUI, WinUI, or Compose kit. I would use it to build the web app’s operation layer, then still need the UI system. Native clients calling that same action runtime would answer the cross-platform objection. Source: [actions overview](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview/).

**CopilotKit** — The shell for putting an agent you already built in front of people: AG-UI, `CopilotSidebar`, shared state, human-in-the-loop, frontend tools, and A2UI surfaces via `create_surface`, `update_components`, and `update_data_model`, either generated by a secondary model or filled into a fixed schema. Frontends named in the README are React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack Block Kit, and Teams Adaptive Cards. That is agent UX across those surfaces, not the app’s design system, and the A2UI styling I read is CSS variables on `.a2ui-surface`. I would sit CopilotKit in front of an agent and still pick Ouro or A2UI for the widgets. A catalog rendered as platform controls, rather than chat CSS, would narrow the gap. Sources: [repository README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [A2UI in CopilotKit](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/generative-ui/a2ui).

**Vercel UI SDK** — A behavior library for coding agents, and a partial runtime bridge for browser agents. `definePrimitive` in `@ui-sdk/core` owns focus, selection, popups, and ARIA; `createParts` renders the same slots in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components. `registerTools` exposes `snapshot`, `act`, and `query` through `document.modelContext`, with an `allow` hook and `consequentialHint` on `act`. The docs index also lists a Mobile section I did not read, so I will not claim the project stops at the browser. What I did read is beta, unstyled, and web-adapter-first. It helps agents build and drive components; it does not give me a visual system or an OS action door. A native part adapter with the same permission hook would make it a contender for the behavior layer under Ouro, not a replacement. Sources: [repository README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui), [WebMCP](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/webmcp).

**shadcn/ui** — Open-code distribution, not a runtime for agents. The CLI copies component source into the app against a flat registry schema, and the docs now include an AI Elements section (Message, Confirmation, Tool, Reasoning) so a model can read and edit the same files a person edits. That is why Ouro HX installs through `shadcn add`. It does not declare agent doors or validate a tree on SwiftUI, WinUI, or Compose. I would keep it as the web distribution mechanism. The missing piece is the action and catalog validator, which is what Ouro adds on top. Source: [documentation](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs).

**AI Elements** — Chat components (Conversation, Message, MessageResponse) copied in via the shadcn CLI, built for the AI SDK. The README says the project will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 and replaced by shadcn/ui’s AI Elements, which the shadcn docs already list. It is a web conversation kit. I would not start a new cross-platform system on this repository; the deprecation note is the objection, and the replacement is already the shadcn registry. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — `@openai/apps-sdk-ui` is a React 18/19 and Tailwind 4 token and component set, built on Radix, with `AppsSDKUIProvider` for router links, aimed at visual consistency inside ChatGPT. I would use it when the only surface is a ChatGPT app and I want that host’s look. It is not a native toolkit and it does not share actions with an agent outside the Apps SDK iframe. MCP Apps is the open version of that host path; this package does not replace a product design system. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui).

**Flutter** — The best write-once human toolkit on the list: one Dart codebase for mobile, web, and desktop, its own widget tree through Skia and Impeller, Material and Cupertino catalogs, and hot reload. An agent reaches it through A2UI’s `a2ui_flutter`, not through anything in the Flutter README. Flutter draws its own controls rather than SwiftUI, WinUI, or Compose, and it has no separate tool door so an agent calls an action instead of tapping a widget. If the app already is Flutter, I would keep it and adopt the A2UI renderer rather than rewrite. That is a codebase constraint, not a reason to choose Flutter for a new dual-use system. Sources: [repository README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter), [A2UI renderer SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Android’s design system, and the look I would expect on that platform: `MaterialTheme`, dynamic color from the wallpaper on Android 12+, a 15-step type scale, tonal elevation, and a large component set including navigation rail, sheets, and adaptive layouts. A2UI’s `material3-a2ui` and Ouro’s Compose kit both sit on Compose. The page I read is theming and components for people; it does not describe an agent calling the same button. I would use Material 3 as Android’s visual contract, not as the cross-platform toolkit. An agent-facing action catalog is outside this document’s scope. Source: [Material Design 3 in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The platform contract for Apple, not a shared toolkit. SwiftUI declares views, scenes, and data flow across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS, and can bridge to UIKit, AppKit, and WatchKit. The HIG is guidance — accessibility, layout, materials, components — not a package an agent composes. Ouro’s Apple kit is SwiftUI because that is how an Apple app should feel. These docs do not cover web, Windows, or Android, and they do not define a generative catalog. I would follow them on Apple and not pretend they are the system. Sources: [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines).

**Tamagui** — A compiler and kit for sharing styled components between React and React Native: `@tamagui/static` flattens styled trees to a `div` plus atomic CSS on web, or a View with hoisted styles on native. That is a serious answer to “one implementation, two renderers,” and the README’s own benchmark is a web homepage, not an agent catalog. I found no action door, consent class, or SwiftUI/WinUI/Compose target in the project README. I would use Tamagui for a human web-and-RN design system. A catalog validator and native-platform kits would be a different product. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui).

**MUI** — A battle-tested React implementation of Material Design, plus MUI X for complex components. I would trust it for a large web app that wants a complete library and a migration path across major versions. The README describes React components and a store of templates; it does not describe agents calling those components or rendering them natively. There is no small fix inside this repository that would make it the dual-use toolkit — the missing layer is an action and catalog model. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui).

**Chakra UI** — Accessible React components on Emotion, including Next.js RSC, with a long component history. The README’s Cursor badge installs `@chakra-ui/react-mcp`, a documentation server for a coding agent. That helps an agent write Chakra; it does not make the running UI an agent surface. It is web-only. I would not choose it for this brief. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui).

**Radix UI** — Unstyled, accessible primitives meant to be the base of a web design system, now MIT-licensed under WorkOS. They are the behavior layer under shadcn and under OpenAI’s Apps SDK UI. The README and docs link are about customization and accessibility on the web. No agent protocol and no native renderer. I would use Radix as a dependency of a web kit, not as the choice. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives).

**Base UI** — Unstyled accessible components from the authors of Radix, Floating UI, and Material UI. The README points at base-ui.com and a release process; it does not describe catalogs, agent tools, or non-React platforms. Same role as Radix: a web primitive layer I might adopt inside a kit, not the system people and agents share across native platforms. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The accessibility bar. React Aria ships more than 50 style-free components with ARIA Authoring Practices behavior, mouse, touch, and keyboard interactions, focus restoration, and internationalization across 30+ languages, 13 calendars, and RTL. React Spectrum is Adobe’s styled system on top; React Stately is the state-hook layer and the repo README notes it can be used independently, including on React Native. I did not find an agent action model or SwiftUI/Compose renderers. If Ouro’s web controls felt wrong under a screen reader, I would want those interactions rebuilt on these hooks. That would answer a quality objection, not the cross-platform agent one. Sources: [repository README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum), [React Aria](https://react-aria.adobe.com/).

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft’s web collection in one repo: React v9 (`@fluentui/react-components`) for Microsoft 365, legacy v8, and web components used by Edge, with Griffel, theming, and an accessibility-by-default stance. This is not WinUI; Ouro’s Windows kit is WinUI 3 for that reason, and Teams Adaptive Cards show up in CopilotKit, not here. I found no agent action model in the Fluent UI README. I would use Fluent for a Microsoft 365 web app. It does not cover the native and agent doors this brief asks for. Source: [repository README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui).

reviews.pullQuote: Ouro UI unifies native human UI, validated agent-composed UI, and auditable agent actions better than any candidate I reviewed.
reviews.testimonial: I would choose Ouro UI because Composed UI turns agent output into validated native component trees, while the one-action model gives people and agents the same governed capability. Its Ouro AX X-ray also checks real CLI, HTTP, and MCP behavior rather than merely documenting conventions. The honest trade-off is ecosystem maturity versus A2UI: Ouro’s native kits and copy-in core adapters are newer and more dispersed, so adopting its conformance matrix is more work than following A2UI’s standalone protocol.
reviews.evaluations:
**Fluent UI** — Fluent v9 is a mature React component suite with a `FluentProvider`, predefined themes, composable components, and separate Web Components, but this repository targets web rather than shared native rendering or an agent interaction model. That makes it a safe enterprise web baseline, while cross-platform agent surfaces would require another protocol and toolkit; the converged v9 package is documented in its [primary README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/fluentui/feab6ba63b55703d803f17092eab54c9dc82430b/packages/react-components/react-components/README.md).

**shadcn/ui** — shadcn distributes owned source rather than a runtime component dependency, and its registry schema explicitly resolves component files, package dependencies, and registry dependencies, which is unusually suitable for customization and coding agents. It is primarily a React/Tailwind delivery architecture with no native renderer or agent-action protocol, so native parity and governance need separate systems; see the [registry schema documentation](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry/registry-json.md).

**MCP Apps** — MCP Apps standardizes a strong boundary: MCP tools declare `ui://` HTML resources, hosts render sandboxed iframes, and views exchange JSON-RPC messages through the host, with declarative CSP and model-versus-app tool visibility. It is excellent for portable chat-host surfaces, but its initial content model is executable HTML rather than native widgets, so it does not itself solve design consistency across SwiftUI or Compose; the architecture and controls are specified in the [MCP Apps overview](https://apps.extensions.modelcontextprotocol.io/api/documents/Overview.html).

**Ouro UI** — Ouro combines a React/SwiftUI/WinUI/Compose native kit with **Composed UI**, whose validated tree can arrive directly, through MCP Apps, or through A2UI; an `ActionButton` inherits consent from the action declaration, so an agent cannot relabel it or weaken confirmation. The **one-action** and **Ouro AX X-ray** model also covers CLI, HTTP, and MCP interfaces, making Ouro unusually complete for both human and agent users; the trade-off is newer, copy-in infrastructure spread across kits and a visible platform conformance matrix, not the single-package maturity of older libraries. Its architecture is concretely described in the [Composed UI guide](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — SwiftUI’s declarative `View` composition, scenes, modifiers, adaptive presentation, model flow, and accessibility integration make it the strongest Apple-native human interface toolkit, while the HIG supplies platform-specific guidance across iOS, macOS, visionOS, watchOS, and tvOS. Its scope is intentionally Apple-only and does not provide a portable agent-generated UI protocol; it remains the native implementation model rather than the cross-platform coordinator, as shown in [Apple’s SwiftUI documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) and [Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/).

**Tamagui** — Tamagui’s compiler lowers shared React components into atomic CSS and flattened DOM on web or React Native views and hoisted styles on mobile, with common tokens, themes, media queries, and accessible primitives. This is one of the best conventional “write once, render web/native” architectures, but it assumes React/React Native and does not define permissions, tool schemas, or agent-facing conformance; its compile-time/runtime split is detailed in the [Tamagui introduction](https://tamagui.dev/unstyled/intro/introduction).

**Chakra UI** — Chakra offers a cohesive web React system built around Panda CSS: `createSystem` compiles typed tokens, semantic tokens, recipes, slot recipes, breakpoints, and CSS variables into a provider-controlled styling engine. It is productive and themeable for web products, but remains a React web library without a native adapter or a boundary for trustworthy model-composed UI; the architecture is documented in the [theming overview](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview).

**AI Elements** — AI Elements provides copy-in React components for AI-specific presentation—messages, conversations, reasoning, queues, and similar interactions—and uses shadcn’s registry workflow, so applications own the resulting code. Its current primary documentation says the project will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 and moved into shadcn, so starting here creates migration uncertainty and it adds no native renderer or agent execution boundary; see the [AI Elements introduction](https://elements.ai-sdk.dev/docs).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — React Aria separates behavior, state, accessibility, localization, and interaction from styling, with render props/slots and over 50 style-free components; React Spectrum is the polished Adobe implementation and React Stately can support other targets. This is a benchmark for accessible web interaction design, but Spectrum itself is not a full native UI stack and no agent protocol is included, so it would need A2UI/MCP/Ouro-style transport above it; the [React Aria documentation](https://react-aria.adobe.com/) is the primary evidence.

**CopilotKit** — CopilotKit is the strongest integration-oriented alternative: framework-native frontends and a server runtime connect to agents over AG-UI, while shared state, frontend tools, human-in-the-loop, and controlled/declarative/open-ended generative UI create a complete user-agent loop. It supports React, Angular, Vue, React Native, and messaging surfaces and can render both A2UI and sandboxed MCP Apps, but it is chiefly an application stack rather than a component vocabulary or native SwiftUI/Compose kit; its three-layer architecture is documented in [CopilotKit’s architecture guide](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/ag2/concepts/architecture).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Agent-Native’s best idea is concrete: one `defineAction` drives React hooks, the model tool, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI through shared schema validation, access checks, and audit behavior; UI state and data are visible to the same action layer, and approvals gate consequential calls. That architecture fits agent-operated business software, but the candidate is a full TypeScript/PostgreSQL application framework, not a portable visual design system or native-rendering toolkit; see the [actions overview](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview/) and [access controls](https://www.agent-native.com/docs/actions-access-control/).

**A2UI** — A2UI defines a transport-decoupled, streaming JSON protocol with strict catalogs, data binding, actions, and bidirectional typed functions, plus React/Angular/Lit, Flutter, and SwiftUI implementations so agents can generate data rather than executable code. That gives it better protocol neutrality than any single UI library and explicit validation boundaries, but catalogs and visual behavior still need host-specific implementation, and the published package list does not presently show a Jetpack Compose package; the [v1.0 specification](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) and [renderer/package overview](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/d4f2761b4629028b7995fdd861a7792eeba529ff/README.md) make the architectural trade-off clear.

**Base UI** — Base UI is an unstyled React library emphasizing accessible WAI-ARIA behavior, broad styling freedom, composable parts, and deliberate browser support; it is a strong primitive layer for a custom web system. It has no visual opinion, native implementation, or agent data/action contract, so selecting it alone would leave the cross-platform and agent halves unsolved; see [Base UI’s about page](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/about).

**MUI** — MUI supplies a comprehensive, production-tested React implementation with self-contained styles, advanced theming, responsive `sx` utilities, and an extensive ecosystem including MUI X. Its web depth is a virtue but also a constraint: it has no native mobile renderer, and the current site says it still adopts Material Design 2 rather than Material 3; the primary [Material UI site](https://mui.com/material-ui/) documents those limits.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Compose Material 3 provides native Android composables, dynamic color, tonal elevation, typography/shape systems, adaptive navigation choices, and built-in platform behavior and accessibility foundations. It is the right Android endpoint but not a web/iOS implementation or an agent protocol; A2UI/json-render trees could supply content, yet the native design language still comes from Compose, as detailed in Google’s [Material 3 in Compose guide](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3).

**json-render** — json-render’s schema/catal­og split constrains generated JSON to predefined components and Zod-validated actions, while its flat tree, state bindings, progressive streaming, and registries for React, React Native, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and other outputs make it exceptionally broad. The flexibility is also its risk: it is a labs framework with application-defined enforcement and renderer quality, and “cross-platform” does not imply native SwiftUI/Compose fidelity; the [README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/json-render/9301e64eb556f972c21eb471ae851603cab65e6b/README.md) and [schema guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/json-render/9301e64eb556f972c21eb471ae851603cab65e6b/apps/web/content/docs/schemas.mdx) expose that contract.

**Vercel UI SDK** — UI SDK cleanly models behavior as framework-neutral primitives—state, API, slots, attributes, press/focus/selection—then maps identical parts to React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components, which is promising for agent-written interaction logic. It does not render native mobile components or supply an agent permission model, and its own documentation marks the SDK beta with changing APIs; see the [UI SDK README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel-labs/ui/ab55044caee66cc8228fa7ed3525088a1b7b5af7/README.md) and [primitive example](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/core/build-a-component).

**Flutter** — Flutter owns a layered rendering engine that targets mobile, web, and desktop from Dart, with Material and Cupertino widget libraries, native embedder services, FFI/platform channels, and hot reload. It offers unusually broad implementation reuse, but its visual output is a common engine rather than each platform’s native toolkit and it lacks a built-in standard for agent UI catalogs, tool authorization, or human approval; Google’s [Flutter architectural overview](https://docs.flutter.dev/resources/architectural-overview) documents the relevant layers.

**Radix UI** — Radix Primitives provides low-level, fully typed React parts with WAI-ARIA behavior, focus management, keyboard navigation, controlled/uncontrolled modes, portals, and the `asChild` composition model, making it a proven foundation for an owned web design system. It is unstyled and web/React-specific, with no native or agent-facing layer, so it solves human interaction behavior only; see the [Radix introduction](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/introduction).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Apps SDK UI offers accessible Radix-based React components, Tailwind 4 integration, design tokens, dark mode, and ChatGPT-optimized layouts with relatively little setup. Its tight host optimization is useful inside ChatGPT but also the limit: it is not a native widget system or an open cross-host protocol, whereas MCP Apps can carry richer standards across compliant hosts; the installation and component architecture are shown in the [primary README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/0f00143c7a639906f1621fe58e1b6be7b5bea46d/README.md).
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines
